title: Grape Downy Mildew (Plasmopara viticola, Oomycota Peronosporaceae)
content: Grape downy mildew, caused by the obligate biotrophic oomycete Plasmopara viticola (Berk. & M.A. Curtis) Berl. & De Toni (Peronosporales, Peronosporaceae, Oomycota, Stramenopiles), is the most devastating foliar and fruit disease of European wine grape (Vitis vinifera L.) cultivars worldwide. Originating in eastern North America where it coevolved with resistant native Vitis species (V. aestivalis, V. labrusca, V. riparia, V. rupestris), P. viticola was accidentally introduced into France in the late 1870s on imported American rootstocks used to replace vines killed by phylloxera; it subsequently spread across the Mediterranean grape-growing regions of Europe, the Middle East, South Africa, South America, Australia, China, and New Zealand over the following 30 years. Today it occurs in all grape-growing regions of the world that receive 100 mm or more of rainfall during the grapevine's active vegetative growth period (April through October in the Northern Hemisphere). Yield and quality losses of 40-90% are recorded annually on susceptible V. vinifera cultivars in wet temperate production areas without adequate chemical protection; in addition to direct berry yield losses, severe premature defoliation weakens vines, reduces fruit ripening and sugar accumulation, increases winter injury, and lowers returns for the following vintage. Downy mildew attacks all green, actively growing grape tissues: leaves, young shoots, petioles, tendrils, inflorescences, and green berries up to the onset of veraison (berry color change and sugar accumulation onset). The first visible symptom on leaves is the appearance of faint, irregularly shaped, bright yellow oily-appearing lesions (called 'oil spots') on the upper leaf surface, limited by veins to poly-angular shapes, typically 5-25 mm across. These oil spot lesions are the diagnostic primary visible symptom on leaves. Under favorable conditions (high RH > 95%, cool temperatures 18-23 C, still nights), within 3-5 days a dense, white to grayish, downy, felt-like growth of sporangiophores and sporangia appears on the corresponding lower (abaxial) leaf surface directly under the oil spots. This 'downy' sporulation is the characteristic from which the disease name derives. With age, the upper-surface oil spots turn necrotic brown, and severely infected leaves curl, wither, and abscise prematurely; complete defoliation can occur within 2-3 weeks in wet seasons. On young shoots, tendrils, petioles, and inflorescence rachises, infection produces slightly swollen, deformed, stunted, yellow-green to brown growth with extensive white downy sporulation on all surfaces; severely infected young shoots often die back from the tip (called 'shepherd's crook' necrosis). On young inflorescences before and shortly after bloom, entire clusters become covered in white downy growth, turn brown, and shrivel completely ('primary cluster blast'), causing 100% crop loss in individual clusters. On green developing berries (from fruit set through the 2-3 mm pea-size stage up to approximately 5-6 weeks post-bloom), infected berries become discolored grayish-brown, develop a thick felt-like white sporulation on their surface, shrivel, dry up, and drop readily from the pedicel. Once berries reach approximately 8-10 Brix (about 5-6 weeks after bloom, beginning of veraison), berries become ontogenically resistant to new P. viticola infection due to accumulation of phenolic and stilbenoid compounds in the berry skin, although the pathogen can still grow systemically through the cluster rachis and pedicels, causing brown 'dry berry rot' (also called leather berry) - necrosis and shriveling of already-formed berries without visible surface sporulation. P. viticola overwinters as thick-walled, spherical, diploid oospores (30-50 um diameter, yellowish-brown wall) in fallen infected grape leaves on the vine floor; oospores survive for up to 5 years. In the spring, beginning at budbreak and continuing through early fruit set, oospores germinate after a minimum 10 mm of rain event combined with soil temperatures above 10 C to produce a single macrosporangium which releases 8-16 biflagellate motile zoospores that swim in free water on the vine floor, are splash-dispersed upward onto the lowest grape leaves by raindrops, encyst on stomata, and penetrate through stomatal openings to establish the first primary leaf lesions (oil spots) of the season. This primary infection from oospores is called the 'rule of 10' (10 C, 10 mm rain, 10 hours leaf wetness, 10 days to first oil spots appearing, in its simplified formulation). Secondary polycyclic inoculum is produced when sporangia, borne on the sporangiophores emerging through stomata from lesions on the lower leaf surface, are wind-dispersed for up to 50-100 km under storm conditions; each sporangium releases 4-8 zoospores that re-infect new leaves, shoots, and clusters through stomata, creating repeated secondary cycles every 5-18 days as long as weather conditions are favorable (night temperatures 15-25 C, minimum 4-6 hours of continuous leaf wetness from dew or rain, RH > 90%). Management: (1) cultural practices: avoid planting susceptible V. vinifera cultivars in low-lying frost pockets, shaded north-facing slopes, or areas with poor air drainage that promote extended dew periods and leaf wetness; train vines to high trellising systems (vertical shoot positioning, bilateral cordon, Scott Henry, Smart-Dyson Ballerina) with wide inter-row spacing (minimum 2.5 m), shoot thinning, leaf removal in the fruit zone (2-3 basal leaves removed at bloom to 2 weeks post-bloom), and shoot positioning to maximize air movement, sunlight penetration, and rapid canopy drying; avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization which promotes extended succulent shoot growth late into the season; cover crops planted between vine rows help reduce splash dispersal of soil-borne inoculum; in organic/low-input systems, remove and destroy heavily infected basal leaves after harvest to reduce overwintering oospore inoculum levels. (2) genetic resistance is the most sustainable long-term approach: American grapevine species (Vitis riparia, V. rupestris, V. aestivalis, V. cinerea, V. berlandieri) carry multiple dominant downy mildew R genes (Rpv1 through Rpv30 characterized) that confer immunity or high-level resistance; European V. vinifera cultivars carry very few functional R genes and are generally highly to extremely susceptible; interspecific hybrid cultivars carrying introgressed Rpv loci (e.g., 'Regent', 'Solaris', 'Cabernet Cortis', 'Bronner', 'Johanniter', 'Souvignier Gris' - the so-called PIWI cultivars - Pilzwiderstandsfahige = fungus-resistant) have been released by European breeding programs and require 60-90% fewer fungicide applications than V. vinifera; cisgenic and transgenic approaches are also being developed to stack multiple Rpv genes without linkage drag from backcrossing. (3) predictive forecasting and decision support systems: because downy mildew infection events are strictly dependent on measurable weather variables (rainfall amount and duration, leaf wetness, temperature), a number of validated forecasting models have been developed and are used operationally by growers: EPIBLAST (France, 1980s), DMCast (Italy/France), iMildew (EU LIFE project), VitiMeteo (France/Germany), and US-based DOWNCAST (Michigan State / Cornell). These models schedule fungicide sprays only when infection risk thresholds are exceeded, typically reducing fungicide use by 30-50% compared to calendar-based protectant programs. (4) chemical fungicide programs (conventional): downy mildew-specific fungicides target the oomycete (Stramenopile) pathogen and are entirely different from the ascomycete/basidiomycete-specific fungicides used for powdery mildew/black rot. The principal FRAC groups used for downy mildew control are: FRAC 4 phenylamides (mefenoxam = metalaxyl-M, the most active curative systemic material ever developed for P. viticola - up to 14 days kickback curative activity; resistance is extremely widespread (MR = 9) in P. viticola populations in all grape-growing regions, so this material is always tank-mixed with a multi-site and limited to maximum 2-3 applications per season; FRAC 40 carboxylic acid amides / CAA (dimethomorph, mandipropamid, iprovalicarb, benthiavalicarb-isopropyl, valifenalate, pyrimorph - protectant + 1-3 day kickback activity; resistance FRAC code 40, moderate risk, limited cross-resistance with some CAAs); FRAC 21 QoI (famoxadone, fenamidone - protectant, resistance risk high since QoI-resistant P. viticola strains are widespread); FRAC 45 ametoctradin (FRAC U8 = new mitochondrial respiration inhibitor; protectant); FRAC 49 oxathiapiprolin (the newest and most active single-site downy mildew material - FRAC 49 = oxysterol binding protein inhibitor; up to 21 days protectant + 3-5 day curative kickback; extremely low use rate); FRAC P07 phosphonates / phosphorous acid / fosetyl-Al (FRAC 33; multi-site mode of action, systemic, stimulates host defense response; moderate protectant + mild curative; no resistance reported after >40 years of use; permitted in many organic programs as potassium phosphite); multi-site FRAC M3 mancozeb, FRAC M1 copper (Bordeaux mixture, copper oxychloride, copper hydroxide, tribasic copper sulfate - these are the backbone protectants in all programs, both conventional and organic, with no resistance risk). All single-site downy mildew fungicides must be alternated between FRAC groups and tank-mixed with multi-site partners to minimize selection pressure for fungicide resistance. (5) organic production programs rely primarily on Bordeaux mixture (copper sulfate + hydrated lime, 10:10:100 formulation) and fixed copper formulations applied every 7-10 days from budbreak through fruit set, plus potassium phosphonate (phosphorous acid) sprays for mild curative kickback. Cupric hydroxide + elemental sulfur + Reynoutria sachalinensis extract rotations provide 55-75% control in moderate to high pressure years compared to the best conventional programs.
